title: Building Color Systems
description: Learn how to build a robust color system that supports light and dark modes. Start with hardcoded colors, refactor into semantic tokens, and create a smooth theme toggle with CSS custom properties and transitions.

steps.title: Start with light-only colors
steps.instruction: Most projects begin with a single set of colors, usually light mode. There is nothing wrong with that—you have to start somewhere. Let's define a straightforward palette with a white background, dark text, and a couple of accent colors.
steps.code: body { background: #ffffff; color: #121726; } .card { background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #e2e5eb; border-radius: 12px; padding: 20px; } .link { color: #3b82f6; }

steps.title: Create semantic color tokens
steps.instruction: The key insight: name colors by purpose, not appearance. Instead of --white and --dark-gray, use --color-surface, --color-text, and --color-border. When you eventually add dark mode, you only need to reassign these tokens—every component updates automatically.
steps.code: :root { /* Surface colors */ --color-bg: #ffffff; --color-surface: #f8f9fa; --color-surface-raised: #ffffff; /* Text colors */ --color-text: #121726; --color-text-secondary: #5a6375; /* Border colors */ --color-border: #e2e5eb; --color-border-strong: #c8ccd4; }

steps.title: Add dark mode with data-scheme
steps.instruction: Now for the magic. By scoping a second set of token values under a [data-scheme="dark"] selector, you create an entirely different visual experience with zero changes to your component CSS. The same --color-surface token just resolves to a different value.
steps.code: /* Light mode (default) */ :root { --color-bg: #ffffff; --color-surface: #f8f9fa; --color-text: #121726; --color-text-secondary: #5a6375; --color-border: #e2e5eb; } /* Dark mode */ [data-scheme="dark"] { --color-bg: #0f1117; --color-surface: #1a1d2b; --color-text: #e8eaed; --color-text-secondary: #8b92a5; --color-border: #2a2d3a; }

steps.title: Build a theme toggle
steps.instruction: Tokens are defined, but users need a way to switch. Let's add a simple toggle button that flips the data-scheme attribute on the document root. A few lines of JavaScript are all it takes to wire up the switch between light and dark.
steps.code: /* Toggle button styles */ .theme-toggle { padding: 8px 16px; border-radius: 20px; border: 1px solid var(--color-border); background: var(--color-surface); color: var(--color-text); cursor: pointer; } /* JavaScript */ toggle.addEventListener('click', () => { const current = document .documentElement .getAttribute('data-scheme'); document.documentElement .setAttribute('data-scheme', current === 'dark' ? 'light' : 'dark' ); });

steps.title: Complete dual-scheme system
steps.instruction: The finishing touch: smooth transitions. By adding a CSS transition to background-color and color on the body and key elements, the scheme change feels intentional rather than jarring. You now have a production-ready color system that mirrors how Figma variables work across modes.
steps.code: /* Smooth transition between schemes */ body { background: var(--color-bg); color: var(--color-text); transition: background-color 0.3s ease, color 0.3s ease; } .card { background: var(--color-surface); border: 1px solid var(--color-border); border-radius: 12px; padding: 20px; transition: background-color 0.3s ease, border-color 0.3s ease; } /* Respect system preference */ @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-scheme]) { --color-bg: #0f1117; --color-surface: #1a1d2b; --color-text: #e8eaed; } }
